title: Methods for uncertainty quantification
text:
The gold standard for inference with error propagation is Bayesian inference which is a from-first-principles approach. Assuming the probability distribution from which the input data are taken is known, one can, using Bayes’ theorem, calculate the probability distribution for the output variable. Hence one would know not only the most probable value, but also the uncertainty of this value.
This takes us back to the fundamental inference problem we really want to solve using an ML model or some other technique. Given a set of possible classes1 and some measurement data, our task is to determine based on the input data which class the instance belong to. One could hope to find some function that gives the answer to this, i.e. \[\text{class} = f(\text{data})\] but in real world problems which are complicated enough that it makes sense to apply machine learning, the input data is insufficient to give a definite output. This could be because of the data being to noisy to determine the output with certainty, but it is also possible that even without the noise more than one class is consistent with the input data.






TipExample



Assume that we want to train a model to determine the occupation of a person. As input we may use data such as educational background, income, age, gender, etc. This should give the model a good chance to achieve a high accuracy, but since there is not one single track to becoming e.g. a software developer a single, predictive function is impossible to find.


The best we can hope for in such cases is to find a probability distribution function which assigns probabilities to the different possible classes, i.e. \[p(\text{class}|\text{data},\text{background knowledge}).\] Here ‘data’ is the measurement data for the instance we are trying to classify, and ‘background knowlege’ is the knowledge we have on the relation between different possible measurement data and the true class.
According to Bayes’ theorem, we can calculate this as \[p(\text{class}|\text{data},\text{background knowledge})
    = \frac{p(\text{class}|\text{background knowledge})p(\text{data}|\text{class},\text{background knowledge})}{p(\text{data}|\text{background knowledge})}
\]
Here \(p(\text{class}|\text{background knowledge})\) is the so-called prior, i.e. the probability we would assign without having the specific information given by the measurement data for that instance. If we know the distribution of the different classes in the population we sample from, we would set the prior equal to that frequency distribution. \(p(\text{data}|\text{class},\text{background knowledge})\) is the probability for observing the measurement data we have given the class we are predicting together with the background knowledge. Finally, \(p(\text{data}|\text{background knowledge})\) is the probability for observing the measurment data given the background knowledge, but not restricting us to a specific class.
Unfortunately, this ideal scenario is not often realised. Even if the input distributions are known, or may be well approximated—which is often the case—the computational cost of integrating over all necessary distributions is prohibitive. In practice one need to resort to some approximation.


BNNs are neural networks in which the weights associated to each node are not single numbers, but probability distributions. In theory, this approach is an example of exact Bayesian inference, but in practice an approximation must be made in the training process. Even with approximations the computational cost of training a BNN is large, making the usability of the approach limited.
Since the weights are replace by probability distributions, the network will produce different outputs if the same instance is fed through it multiple times. The spread of the outputs may be used as and estimate of the epistemic uncertainty of the model.



Monte Carlo dropout is an alternative to BNN with a much lower computational cost. It can be proved to be equivalent to BNN in certain cases,2 but also for many cases where the proof does not apply, experience indicates that the method yields resonable uncertainty estimates.
Monte Carlo dropout is a well known technique for regularization of NNs. By randomly removing some of the connections between nodes at each pass during training, single nodes or groups of nodes are less likely to dominate the inference made by the NN reducing the tendency to overtraining. The same technique is now used, but at inference-time. I.e. after training the network, inference is repeated multiple times with Monte Carlo dropout activated. This results in a spread in the output of the NN which can be used to estimate the epistemic uncertainty.

Propagation of aleatoric uncertainty
The metods described above are mostly concerned with the uncertainty related to the ML model itself (epistemic), although versions of some of them can also estimate the aleatoric3 uncertainty, a more straight-forward approach is to estimate the uncertainty of the input data (which is usually done anyway) and then propagate it through the ML model—similar to the approach described in the introduction to this chapter. Different approaches to this propagation has been proposed, for example [Jungmann2024]4 which shows that it can be done (at least if correlations are negligible) in a computationally efficient manner which has a close connection to the procedure used for analytical functions.

title: Summary of Module B
text: The red thread of the module has been to have a critical look at how we evaluate the outcome of any machine learning model to ensure that we can trust its output/decision. A machine learning model may look impressive with a high accuracy, but still be completely useless. Whether you are developing or using models, it is important to make sure that the model you are working with is robust and trusthworthy—not only gives impressive stats on some test data set.

title: Metrics
text: To quantify how well a ML model performs, and to compare it to other models, we need a quantitative metric. Many such metrics are possible, but not all are equally good - and more importantly a good metric for one problem isn’t necessarily a good metric for the next problem. In order to select an appropriate metric for a specific problem, you would both need to know the characteristics of different possible metrics as well as details about the problem you are working on.

title: Iris regression with a small neural network
text:
Predict petal width (cm) from the other three measurements: sepal length, sepal width and petal length.
Network: 3 inputs → hidden layer(s) → 1 output (linear), ReLU activations, trained with Adam on squared error. A plain linear regression serves as a baseline.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, r2_score
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPRegressor
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

title: Iris regression with a small neural network
text:
Settings
Use (16,) for one hidden layer or (16, 8) for two.

HIDDEN_LAYERS = (16, 8)   # two hidden layers: 16 and 8 neurons
SEED = 42

title: Iris regression with a small neural network
text:
Data
Columns 0–2 (sepal length, sepal width, petal length) are the inputs; column 3 (petal width) is the target. The split is stratified by species so all three are represented in both sets.

iris = load_iris()
X = iris.data[:, :3]
y = iris.data[:, 3]
feature_names = iris.feature_names[:3]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.3, stratify=iris.target, random_state=SEED
)
print("Inputs:", feature_names)
print(f"Train: {X_train.shape[0]} samples, test: {X_test.shape[0]} samples")

Inputs: ['sepal length (cm)', 'sepal width (cm)', 'petal length (cm)']
Train: 105 samples, test: 45 samples

title: Iris regression with a small neural network
text:
Models
Both models see standardized inputs. The neural network uses a linear output unit and minimizes squared error; a little L2 regularization (alpha) keeps the weights small.

mlp = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    MLPRegressor(
        hidden_layer_sizes=HIDDEN_LAYERS,
        activation="relu",
        solver="adam",
        learning_rate_init=0.01,
        alpha=1e-3,
        max_iter=2000,
        random_state=SEED,
    ),
)
linear = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LinearRegression())

mlp.fit(X_train, y_train)
linear.fit(X_train, y_train)
print("Both models trained.")

Both models trained.

title: Iris regression with a small neural network
text:
Evaluation
RMSE is in centimetres; R² is the fraction of variance in petal width explained.

def report(name, model):
    pred_train = model.predict(X_train)
    pred_test = model.predict(X_test)
    rmse_train = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_train, pred_train))
    rmse_test = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, pred_test))
    print(f"{name:<18} train RMSE {rmse_train:.3f}  test RMSE {rmse_test:.3f}  "
          f"test R² {r2_score(y_test, pred_test):.3f}")
    return pred_test

print(f"Target range: {y.min():.1f}–{y.max():.1f} cm, std {y.std():.3f} cm\n")
pred_mlp = report(f"MLP {HIDDEN_LAYERS}", mlp)
pred_lin = report("Linear regression", linear)

Target range: 0.1–2.5 cm, std 0.760 cm

MLP (16, 8)        train RMSE 0.182  test RMSE 0.206  test R² 0.920
Linear regression  train RMSE 0.185  test RMSE 0.203  test R² 0.922

title: Iris regression with a small neural network
text:
Predicted vs. actual
Points on the dashed line are perfect predictions. Colours show species.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.5), sharex=True, sharey=True)
_, _, _, species_test = train_test_split(
    X, iris.target, test_size=0.3, stratify=iris.target, random_state=SEED
)
lims = [y.min() - 0.2, y.max() + 0.2]
for ax, pred, title in [(axes[0], pred_mlp, "Neural network"), (axes[1], pred_lin, "Linear regression")]:
    for k, name in enumerate(iris.target_names):
        m = species_test == k
        ax.scatter(y_test[m], pred[m], label=name, alpha=0.8)
    ax.plot(lims, lims, "k--", lw=1)
    ax.set(xlim=lims, ylim=lims, xlabel="Actual petal width (cm)", title=title)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Predicted petal width (cm)")
axes[0].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Classification of uncertainty
text: Before continuing the discussion how to quantify the uncertainty, let’s start by having a look of different types of uncertainty. Depending on the domain, there are different ways of classifying uncertainty, which are only partly overlapping. Here, I will discuss two types of classifications. In many natural sciences, e.g. physics, one usually talks about statistical/stochastic and systematic uncertainty. In computer science one more often refer to aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. These two classification schemes are often described as indentical making statistical—aleatoric and systematic—epistemic synonyms. In reality there are however some subtle differences, since the nature of uncertainty in a physical measurement and in a mathematical model are different.

title: Classification of uncertainty
text:
Statistical/stochastic uncertainty
If we repeat a measurement, say the voltage across a light bulb, several times we will not get the same value every time (provided the resolution of the voltmeter is sufficently good) since the voltage can never be absolutely stable. In the same way, if we measure the time interval between radioactive decays from some source, there will be some variation since the decay process is fundamentally stochastic. The same is true for any physical measurement - if you try to make it sufficiently precise, you will necessarily observe some fluctuations in the value you measure. The statistical uncertainty is relatively easy to handle: by making repeated measurements and averaging the result one find a better estimate of the true value than what a single measurement will give. Also, if one has some knowledge of the underlying statistical model for the fluctuations (Gaussian, Poisson, …) there are concrete receipts on how to quantify the uncertainty of this estimate. Furthermore, if one calculates a quantity which is a function of two or more measured values, the uncertainty of the compund quantity can easily(ish) be calculated as well, as described in the previous section.
The statistical uncertainty can always be reduced by adding more data—the magnitude of the uncertainty scales as \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\) where \(N\) is number of measurements. However, given it’s random nature one cannot reduce the impact of statistical uncertainty beyond a certain point by processing the data in a more clever way. For this reason, it is often referred to as an irreducible uncertainty.

title: Classification of uncertainty
text:
Systematic uncertainty
Systematic uncertainties relates to specific measurement apparatuses or procedures, and countrary to the statistical uncertainty will typically shift all measurement results in one direction. A trivial example may be a measurement rod which expands or contracts when the temperature changes. All measurements taken at the same temperatur will then be shifted by the same amount. There is no general procedure for how to estimate the systematic uncertainty - it depends too much on the nature of the measurement that is done. In many cases the best one can do is to perform the same measurement with a different apparatus/procedure and use the deviation as an estimate of the uncertainty. Also, there is no general prescription for how to combine the statistical uncertainty into a compound uncertainty when calculating a value based on several measured parameters. It is quite common to use the same procedure as for statistical uncertainties, but there is no statistical foundation for doing this.
Increasing the amount of data will in general not reduce the size of the systematic uncertainty. However, having more data at your disposal may in some cases allow you to improve measurements that again can let you reduce the systematic uncertainty.

title: Classification of uncertainty
text:
Aleatoric uncertainty
In the context of ML, aleatoric uncertainty is the uncertainty on the data which are used as input to the ML model. Making the connection to the statistical—systematic split of uncertainty, all statistical uncertainty is aleatoric, but not necessarily all systematic uncertainty. In general, there will be a systematic uncertainty connected to the measurement of the input values—and this \(will\) contribute to the aleatoric uncertainty. The choise of model, an specific choises of hyperparameters will also contribute a systematic uncertainty, but this should be regarded as part of the epistemic uncertainty which is discussed in the next paragraph.

title: Classification of uncertainty
text:
Epistemic uncertainty
Epistemic uncertainty is in some sense also a systematic uncertainty, but usually referes only to uncertainties relating to the model which is used to analyse the data.






TipExample



In the example from the previous section, the expression relating \(T\), \(L\) and \(g\), \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\), is not quite precise but is only an approximation to a much more complicated expression. First of all, the expresision is derived assuming that all of the mass in the pendulum is located in a point at the end of the string. This is of course not true (but may be an ok approximation in some cases). Secondly, the derivation uses \(\sin\theta \simeq \theta\) which only is true in the limit \(\theta\to 0\). As is typical for an epistemic uncertainty, it can be reduced1 by improving the mathematical model that is used.


When using a complex ML model like a deep NN, there is still the possibility that the model cannot adequately describe the relation we are trying to find. Due to the complexity–and opaqueness–of the ML model it is much harder in this case to evaluate how large of an epistemic uncertainty we have, and to find out how to reduce it if necessary.

title: Classification of uncertainty
text:
Out-of-distribution data
If an instance which is not represented by the training data is fed through the trained ML model, most models will produce a prediction just as it would for any other instance. However, since this involves an extrapolation outside of domain from which we have information this inference will naturally come with an additional uncertainty on top of the usual set of uncertainties involved in the inference. This kind of uncertainty is often not discussed, but is important to include since it may be very large and difficult to quantify. In general one would expect the out-of-distribution uncertainty to grow with increasing distance to the training data, and as such a successful estimation of this uncertainty could be usable as an anomaly detector, flagging data not consistent with the training data set by assigning a particularly large uncertainty.
This source of uncertainty is often neglected in the discussion of uncertainty quantification, and according to [Everett2022]2 common approaches to estimating the uncertainty of an ML model fail to yield reasonable estimates for this important case, particularly if the model is also required to give a very low false positive rate—which is often required for ML models that should be deployed into practical use.
For out-of-distribution data, there are two different cases which requires different handling. First there is “clean data”, meaning that all the input features of the instance have plausible values, but (some of which) are out of the range represented in the training data. Say, we have an image classifier trying to determine bird species. If the classifier was never trained on images of gulls, it cannot be expected to recognize gull images even though the images are of perfect quality. The best we can hope for is that it returns ‘no known class’, or if this is not an option it should return some class, but with very large uncertainty. Secondly there is “adverserial data”. This is an input instance specially designed to fool the classifier. Ideally, also this should come out as ‘no known class’ or some class, but with a large error.

title: Classification of uncertainty
text:
Footnotes


But it cannot be completely removed since the equation describing the pendulum doesn’t have an analytic solution. This is no problem, however, since there will allways be statistical errors present as well. When the epistemic uncertainty is reduced to be much smaller than the systematic error one doesn’t gain anything from further reducing it.↩︎
Improving Out-of-Distribution Detection via Epistemic Uncertainty Adversarial Training, D Everett et al., arXiv:2209.03148 (2022)↩︎

import numpy as np # linear algebra
import struct

#
# MNIST Data Loader Class

class MnistDataloader(object):
    def __init__(self, training_images_filepath,training_labels_filepath,
                 test_images_filepath, test_labels_filepath):
        self.training_images_filepath = training_images_filepath
        self.training_labels_filepath = training_labels_filepath
        self.test_images_filepath = test_images_filepath
        self.test_labels_filepath = test_labels_filepath
    
    def read_images_labels(self, images_filepath, labels_filepath):        
        labels = []
        with open(labels_filepath, 'rb') as file:
            magic, size = struct.unpack(">II", file.read(8))
            if magic != 2049:
                raise ValueError('Magic number mismatch, expected 2049, got {}'.format(magic))
            labels = array("B", file.read())        
        
        with open(images_filepath, 'rb') as file:
            magic, size, rows, cols = struct.unpack(">IIII", file.read(16))
            if magic != 2051:
                raise ValueError('Magic number mismatch, expected 2051, got {}'.format(magic))
            image_data = array("B", file.read())        
        images = []
        for i in range(size):
            images.append([0] * rows * cols)
        for i in range(size):
            img = np.array(image_data[i * rows * cols:(i + 1) * rows * cols])
            img = img.reshape(28, 28)
            images[i][:] = img            
        
        return images, labels
            
    def load_data(self):
        x_train, y_train = self.read_images_labels(self.training_images_filepath, self.training_labels_filepath)
        x_test, y_test = self.read_images_labels(self.test_images_filepath, self.test_labels_filepath)
        return (x_train, y_train),(x_test, y_test)

title: Calibration methods
text:
Most calibration methods for ML models are post-hoc, i.e. the model is first trained without calibration in mind and only after that the model output is calibrated to try to align the model confidence with the true posterior probability. Defining “true posterior probability” properly may be difficult, but for the purpose of this section we shall adopt the definition that true posterior probability is the frequency found in a representative test set. I.e., if we select instances classified to have a confidence in a narrow range around \(\alpha\), then the fraction of correctly classified events should be \(\alpha\) if the model is properly calibrated.
Schematically, the goal of the calibration is to move from the plot on the left to the plot on the right. On the left is a situation which seems to be typical for the complex neural networks that have become popular recently. The confidence is boosted such that allmost all of the correctly classified instances come with a very high confidence. If one measures the average confidence this comes out as (much larger) than the accuracy. The plot to the right shows an ideal case, where there is an excellent correspondance between confidence and accuracy.

The presention of calibration methods below is based on [Guo2017]1 where also more details can be found.


Define bin boundaries \(0=b_1\leq b_2 \leq \ldots \leq b_{M+1} = 1\) such that classified2 instances are put in mutually exclusive bins. There is no hard rule on how to choose the bin boundaries, but typically one would either choose uniform bin width or (approximately) equal number of instances per bin. For each bin, the calibrated confidence is determined to be the value \(\theta_m\) that minimizes the squared loss of the instances in the bin: \[\min_{\theta_m} \sum_{i=1}^{n}(\theta_m - y_i)^2\] where \(y_i \in \{0,1\}\) is the target value for instance \(i\).



This is a generalisation of the histogram binning approach where also the binning is subject to opitmization. In specific, let the calibrated confidences per bin \(\theta_m\) be determined by minimising \[
\min_{\stackrel{M}{\stackrel{\theta_1,\ldots\theta_M}{b_1\ldots b_{M+1}}}}
\sum_{m=1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{N}{\mathbf I}(b_i\leq \hat{p}_i < b_{i+1}) (\theta_m-y_i)^2
\] subject to \(0=b_1\leq b_2 \leq \ldots \leq b_{M+1} = 1\) and \(\theta_1 \leq\theta_2\leq\ldots\theta_M\). Here \(\hat{p_i}\) is the ML model’s (pre-calibration) confidence of instance \(p_i\), and \({\mathbf I}(\cdot)\) is the indicator function. Thus each instance contribute to the sum, only in the bin where it belongs. Note that in this approach both number of bins as well as the different bin widths are determined through the minimisation procedure.



This is another generalisation of histogram binning which is based on Bayesian model averaging. Instead of, like isotonic regression, just letting the selected binning be subject to optimisation BBQ considers all possible binnings that respect the constraint \(0=b_1\leq b_2 \leq \ldots \leq b_{M+1} = 1\) simultaneously and averages over the probabilities given by each binning. The weights used in the averaging are found using Bayes’ rule.



This is a standard linear regression applied to the predictions of the pre-calibrated ML model. Let \(z_i\) be the confidence before calibration. Post-calibration confidences are then calculated as \[\hat{q}_i = \sigma(az_i + b)\] where \(\sigma(\cdot)\) is the standard sigmoid function and the parameters \(a\) and \(b\) are optimized using the validation set.

title: Calibration methods
section: Challenges when extending to multiclass calibration
text:
Challenges when extending to multiclass calibration
In a multiclass setting, the ML model outputs one confidence per class per instance, i.e. the prediction for an instance may be \[ [0.73, 0.06, 0.13, 0.08]\] signinfying that the model holds highest confidence to placing the instance in the first class, but the other classes are also possible. What do we expect from the calibration? Should only the confidence of the most probable class be “correct”? Or should we require all classes to have “correct” confidence? Multiple definitions of calibration are possible. Following [Perez-Lebel2023]3 we consider three different definitions. In all the definitions, let \(s = (s_1,\ldots, s_k)\) be the per-class confidence scores and \(\{e_1, \ldots ,e_K\}\) be the set of all one-hot vectors of size K4.
With these definitions \(P(Y=e_k|S=s)\) should be read as the probability for the true value of the instance being class \(k\) given that the ML model produces the confidence score vector \(s\).
Joint calibration5 is the strongest of the three definitions and requires \[P(Y=e_k|S = s) = s_k \quad\text{for}\quad k=1,\ldots,K\] i.e., we require that all of the confusion matrix is properly calibrated.
A slightly weaker definition is class-wise calibration where we require \[P(Y=e_k|S_k = s_k) = s_k \quad\text{for}\quad k=1,\ldots,K.\] i.e., we no longer require that all of the confusion matrix is properly calibrated, but only the confidences for the class the element actually belongs to.
An even weaker definition is top-label calibration where we require \[P(Y=e_{\mathrm{argmax}(s)}|\max(S) = s) = s \quad\text{for}\quad k=1,\ldots,K\] i.e., we require only that the probability for the class with highest confidence is correct.

title: Bayesian Inference
text:
Even if information we have is insufficient to determine what class an instance belong to, we can still hope to calculate probabilities for it belonging to the various possible clases. I.e. we want to calculate: \[P(\text{class}|\text{data},\text{background knowledge}).\] Here ‘data’ is the measurement data for the instance we are trying to classify, and ‘background knowlege’ is any other relevant knowledge we have, including on the relation between different possible measurement data and the true class.
According to Bayes’ theorem, we can calculate this as \[P(\text{class}|\text{data},\text{background knowledge})
    = \frac{P(\text{class}|\text{background knowledge})P(\text{data}|\text{class},\text{background knowledge})}{P(\text{data}|\text{background knowledge})}
\]
Here \(P(\text{class}|\text{background knowledge})\) is the so-called prior, i.e. the probability we would assign without having the specific information given by the measurement data for that instance. If we know the distribution of the different classes in the population we sample from, we would set the prior equal to that frequency distribution. \(P(\text{data}|\text{class},\text{background knowledge})\) is the probability for observing the measurement data we have given the class we are predicting together with the background knowledge. Finally, \(P(\text{data}|\text{background knowledge})\) is the probability for observing the measurment data given the background knowledge, but not restricting us to a specific class.
If either the class and/or the data is replaced by a continuous variable, the expression above needs to be modified slightly. Let \(p(\theta|x)\) be the probability density function (p.d.f.) describing the probability for observing a certain value of the parameter(s) of interest, \(\theta\), given data \(x\) (which usually will be multi-dimensional). The probability will still also depend on the background knowledge, but this denpendency is supressed to de-clutter the notation. Bayes’ formula for this case is: \[
    p(\theta|x) = \frac{p(x|\theta)p(\theta)}{\int p(x|\theta)p(\theta)\mathrm{d}\theta}
\] which has the same interpretation as the version above. I.e., \(p(x|\theta)\) is the probability for the observation we have made (\(x\)) given that the parameter(s) of interest are \(\theta\), \(p(\theta)\) is the probility for the parameter(s) of interest being \(\theta\) prior to the extra information provided by observing \(x\), and the integral in the denominator is the probability for observing \(x\) irrespective of the value of \(\theta\).
If the goal is to determine the value of \(\theta\) we are basically done now.1 Of course we can refine our determination of \(\theta\) by performing more observations and repeat the procedure. However, we are often not primarily interested in determining the value of \(\theta\), but in predicting the value \(\tilde{x}\) of a new observation given the information we have already gathered through observations \(\mathbf{x} = \{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\). This can be calculated as \[
    p(\tilde{x}|\mathbf{x}) = \int p(\tilde{x}|\theta)p(\theta|\mathbf{x})\mathrm{d}\theta
\] Where \(p(\theta|\mathbf{x})\) is the result of the calculation using Bayes’ formula above (possibly multiple times to include several observations).

title: Calibration
text:
A machine learning model for classification typically output a value (or one value per class for multiclass classification) which is used to determine the predicted class. In the case of binary classification, one typically apply a threshold such that if the number is above threshold the instance is predicted to belong to the positive class. For multiclassification, one typically choose the class associated with the largest output. Instead of only using a threshold or the class with the largest output number one can try to extract more informantion from the output value itself. Assume that the value is in the range [0,1].1 The closer to 1, the more confident we can be in the classification.
Allthough the output cannot be interpreted as probability there is often (but not always) a one-to-one relation between the output value and the true probability. To obtain the probability from the ML output, one can apply a calibration step after training the ML model.
Some years ago there was observed a trend2 that the developments in ML over the past years that had produced a much better accuracy at the same time tend to lead to more mis-calibrated results out of the box. Later development has made this trend less clear, and the degree of mis-calibration seems to be, among other things, dependent on which kind of model is used3

title: Calibration
text:
The need for calibration
The importance of calibration depends a lot on the usecase of the ML model. For example, if the ML model is to be used in a decision theoretical context where one need to calculate the expected utililty, it is clearly critical that the model is properly calibrated. On the other hand, in a recommandation system where one may only care about picking the best candidate it is not obvious that proper calibration is critical.

        self.dropout2 = nn.Dropout(0.5)

        x = self.conv2(x)
        x = F.relu(x)
        x = F.max_pool2d(x, 2)
        x = self.dropout1(x)
        x = torch.flatten(x, 1)
        x = self.fc1(x)
        x = F.relu(x)
        x = self.dropout2(x)
        x = self.fc2(x)
        output = F.log_softmax(x, dim=1)
        return output

title: Grouping loss
text:
Even if the ML algorithm is well calibrated overall, it is not guaranteed that the confidence for individual instances is well matched with the true probability for its classification. Before attempting a more general discussion, lets consider an example.






TipExample



The CIFAR-10 dataset consists of 60000 (training) + 10000 (test) 32x32 pixel colour images organised into 10 non-overlapping categories. Using a quite small NN, the images are categorised with 71% accuracy. To check how well calibrated the NN is, we plot the fraction of correctly classified images as a function of NN output (20 bins). With a perfectly calibrated NN, the fraction should correspond to NN output, i.e. all points should be on the dashed line. The size of error bars in the plots are calculated assuming a Poisson distribution (which we will se is not appropriate in this example)

Except for the three first bins, which are empty, the NN agreement with the dashed line is very good. We could therefore be tempted to conclude that this is a well-calibrated NN and move on. But things are not so simple. Even though the NN is well calibrated on average, this does not need to be the case for each individual prediction. Thus even though 70% of all images with output 0.7 indeed are correctly classified, it may be - and in this case are - subsets of images with NN output 0.7 where the fraction of correctly classified images deviate a lot from 70%.
If we now make the same plot, but restricted to data belonging to only one category things look different. For instance classification of images which really belongs to category 5 (dogs) still look pretty good, but for category 3 (cats) the fraction of correctly classified images is much lower than the “probability” found by the NN.
 
Making the same plot for all 10 categories (hiding the errorbars to de-clutter the plot) shows that the spread is quite large. Thus, even though the NN output on average had a good match to the probability for the image to be classified correctly, on an category by category basis this is far from true. What hasn’t been checked here, but is conceivable, is that there are also variations within the categories. It could for instance be that only a subset of the cat images are classified with too low confidence, while another subset has correct or even too high confidence.

title: Introduction
text:
There are a large number of tools that let you easily set up and train a neural network or other machine learning (ML) model to analyse a data set. Such models may give good results, but to understand whether they really do, a critical evaluation should be performed. We will see that an ML model may classify over 99% of all instances correct, and still be completely useless. In other cases 80% correct may be a great result. It all depends on the problem at hand - and it is critical to consider the nature of the problem when evaluating what is a good result. The first part of this module will discuss how to evaluate the performance of a trained ML model.
Typically in a classification task, the final layer applies a sigmoid (or softmax if multiclass) function that transforms the output to a number between 0 and 1. This number is often interpreted as a probability for the instance to belong to a certain class, but this is generally not true. Allthough a well-trained model should output a number which is such that closer to 1 means more probable to be of that class, there is no reason to expect a linear relation between the ML output and the probability of belonging to the class. If the exact probability isn’t of importance to us, we may get away with using the ML output as it is - but remember to not confuse it with a probability. However, there are many cases where “more likely to be of this class” isn’t good enough. In such cases we can attempt to calibrate the output to actually approximate the true probability. This discussion is the topic of the second part of the module.
Assume you have a well-trained, well-calibrated ML model. If the model outputs 90% probability for an instance to belong to class A, are you then sure that you can trust this number? In general there are a lot of sources of uncertainty/randomness, both relating to measurement of the input features used in training the model, in selection of training data, and in the process of setting up and training the ML model. If the classification is important, we should not only care about the probability assingned by the model, but also how certain this probability is. Whether an instance is evaluated to belong to class A with \((90\pm 1)\%\) probability or with \((90^{+10}_{-30})\%\) probability may make a major difference. This discussion is the topic of the third part of the module.

title: Loss function, metric and utility
text: Loss function, metric and utility are related, but still different concepts that are used when developing a machine learning model. The former two are best known, and are generally discussed in any introduction to machine learning. The latter is less often discussed, but should not be forgotten when creating a machine learning model which is to be used for decision making. The same mathematical function may be used for all three, but more typically one will use different functions for each of them.

title: Loss function, metric and utility
text:
Loss function
The role of the loss function is to measure the performance of the machine learning model during training, to guide the further training process. For example in the case of supervised learning, the loss function is a quantitative measure of the difference between the machine learning model’s prediction on (a batch of) the training data and the ground truth of the same dataset. Thus the training proceeds by trying to minimize the loss function. In order for a loss function to work well in the optimisation procedure it needs to be as close to continous as possible. To understand why, it is easiest to first consider a counter-example. Let’s say we use the precision, \[\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+TN}\] as loss function in a classification problem. Here TP and TN are the number of true positives (instances correctly classified to the class we denote as positive) and true negatives (instances correctly classified to the class we denote negative), respectively. For this proposed loss function to change its value, the parameters of the model must be changed enough to change the classification of at least one event, thus increasing or decreasing TP or TN. In many cases this may require a substantial change in parameters, causing the training process to stop prematurely. A more commonly used, and better loss function for classification is the cross entropy \[H = -y\log\hat{y} - (1-y)\log(1-\hat{y})\] where \(y = 0 \text{ or } 1\) denominates the true class of the instance, whereas \(0\leq \hat{y} \leq 1\) is the model’s prediction of the same instance. Comparing to the Precision case above, the value of \(\hat{y}\) would have to cross a threshold (ofte taken to be \(0.5\)) for the loss function to change its value. However, in this case any change in the value of \(\hat{y}\) would change the value of the loss function.

title: Loss function, metric and utility
text:
Metric
The role of the metric is to measure the performance of the trained machine learning model, and to allow for comparison of the performance across different models applied to the same task. The metric should not just be any number which can measure the performance, but it should ideally be easy to interpret the meaning of its numerical value. Furthermore, the measure should be chosen to be meaningful for the type of data, and in the relevant context the machine learning model is applied to. This latter point will be the topic of the next section, and will thus not be discussed here. But it can be useful to briefly look at why a typical loss function such as cross entropy is normally not well suited as a metric. After all, the loss function is also a meaure of the model’s performance, so one might wonder why not let it also be our metric. First of all, the cross entropy as defined above, was presented per evaluated instance. Thus to evaluate the performance on a larger batch of instances, one would sum over all individual contributions. This means that the value of the cross entropy depends on the batch size, so one would at least have to normalise it to get a meaningful value for comparison. But the cross entropy also depends on the exact values of \(\hat{y}\) from the model. Two models which perform equally well measured by other means can have very different \(\hat{y}\)-distributions. Thus for a comparison across different model architectures, the cross entropy (and most other typical loss functions) is not well suited. Furthermore, different types of machine learning models (neural networks, support vector machines, regression trees, etc.) may have different optimal, or even possible, loss functions - again showing that the loss function is usually not a good choise as metric.

title: Loss function, metric and utility
text:
Utility
The utility measures the “value” of the outcome of the decision made by the machine learning model; for instance how much money is won or lost by making that decision. Thus the decision process should be set up such that the expected utility is maximised. Maximising the utility is not necessarily equivalent to optimising one of the metrics which is typically used for evaluating model performance.






TipExample



As an example of this, let’s imagine a test that determines whether maintenance of some machinery is required. There is a cost to performing maintenance, but failing to maintain the machinery when needed will cause a breakdown that is much more expensive. Define positive = test claims that maintenance is required and negative = test claims that maintenance is not required. Assume that the associated costs are (in some arbitrary units):

Furthermore, let’s assume that at some particular time the probability that maintenance is in fact required is 5%.
If we assume our test to be 97% accurate, we can calculate the expected cost as: \[\begin{align*}
        E[U] &= \text{ACC}\cdot(f_\text{pos}\cdot U_\text{TP} + f_\text{neg}\cdot U_\text{TN}) + (1-\text{ACC})\cdot(f_\text{neg}\cdot U_\text{FP} + f_\text{pos}\cdot U_\text{FN}) \\
        &= 0.97\cdot [0.05\cdot (-1) + 0.95\cdot 0] + 0.03\cdot[0.95\cdot(-1) + 0.05\cdot(-1000)] \\
        &= -1.577

If one, on the other hand, we don’t use the test at all and just classify everyting as positive - meaning we perform maintenance every time - the expected cost is: \[\begin{align*}
        E[U] &= f_\text{pos}\cdot U_\text{TP} + f_\text{neg}\cdot U_\text{FP} \\
        &= 0.05\cdot (-1) + 0.95\cdot (-1) \\
        &= -1
    \end{align*}\] which is less expensive than the result using the test. So we see that the large cost of false negatives means that not even a 97% accurate model is sufficient to beat always choosing positive class. In fact, the test would need to have an accuracy of 98.1% to break even.


One can of course choose the utility as the metric for the ML model (or rather -utility since the standard convention is that we want to maximize utility and minimize the metric). Doing it this way may be a good option, but in most1 cases this is not necessary as one can get equally good results by maximizing the performance using another relevant metric, and then calculating the utility at the end.

title: Evaluation metrics
text: Before discussing how to chose an appropriate metric for the problem at hand, let’s start by defining the most commonly used metrics for classification and regression problems, respectively.

title: Evaluation metrics
text:
Metrics for binary classification
An ML model typically gives out a score for each instance which is the basis for the classification. Often this score is normalised to be in the range [0,1] where we take numbers closer to 0 to mean classified as belonging to the negative class, and numbers closer to 1 mean classified as belonging to the positive class. Often, but not necessarily, the threshold is placed at 0.5.

Confusion matrix
The most commonly used metrics for classification are based on the confusion matrix. The confusion matrix for binary classification is a \(2\times 2\) matrix categorising the classified events as:

True positive (TP) if the instance was classified as belonging to the positive class and this was correct.
True negative (TN) if the instance was classified as belonging to the negative class and this was correct.
False positive (FP) if the instance was classified as belonging to the positive class and this was incorrect.
False negative (FN) if the instance was classified as belonging to the negative class and this was incorrect.

There is no universally adopted convention for whether rows or columns should present the actual value, so it is important that the axes on the confusion matrix are labelled.

The numbers in the confusion matrix may be presented in different ways: Commonly the absolute numbers for each category is presented, but it is often beneficial to also include relative numbers. The normalisation of the relative numbers may differ, so pay attention! The numbers for all of the matrix may sum to 1, or each row or column may sum to 1.



Scalar metrics
Based on the numbers from the confusion matrix, we can define several scalars which are measures of performance. Since we are reducing the \(2\times2\) matrix into a scalar, some information is necessarily lost. With an appropriate choice of metric, this loss of information isn’t a problem, but choosing a metric which doesn’t fit the problem at hand will yield a misleading measure of performance.

Accuracy is a measure of the fraction of correctly classified instances \[\text{Accuracy} = \frac{TP + TN}{P + N} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + FP  + TN + FN}\]
Precision is a measure of how large a fraction classified as positive was correctly classified \[\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}\]
True positive rate (TPR), recall or sensitivity is a measure of how large a fraction of the positive class was correctly classified \[\text{TPR} = \frac{TP}{P} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}\]
True negative rate (TNR), Specificity is a measure of how large a fraction of the negative class was correctly classified \[\text{TNR} = \frac{TN}{N} = \frac{TN}{TN + FP}\]
F1 score is the most commonly used member of a more general class of measures (F\(\beta\) score) and is defined as the harmonic mean of precision and recall \[\text{F}_1 = \left( \frac{\frac{1}{\text{precision}}+\frac{1}{\text{recall}}}{2}\right)^{-1} = 2\frac{\text{precision}\cdot\text{recall}}{\text{precision+recall}} = \frac{2TP}{2TP + FP + FN}\] By choosing \(\beta \neq 1\) one can give more weigth to either precision or recall \[\text{F}_\beta = (1+\beta^2)\frac{\text{precision}\cdot\text{recall}}{(\beta^2\cdot\text{precision)+recall}} = \frac{(1+\beta^2)TP}{(1+\beta^2)TP + FP + \beta^2FN}\]




Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve
By computing a single scalar as the above metrics are examples of, we discard a lot of information that may be useful for the user of the ML model. An alternative that preserves some of that information is the ROC curve. This is a plot of true postitive rate vs false positive rate.

The diagonal gray line is the ROC curve of blind guessing. The higher above the diagonal, the better - so in this example, the classifier represented by the blue curve is better than the classifier represented by the red curve. By presenting the performance of the classifier by an ROC curve, the user can choose “working point” according to their need - whether they need to prioritize a high true positive rate (retain a lot of the signal) or a low false positive rate (avoid a lot of background masking the signal).
By integrating the ROC one obtain the area under the (ROC) curve, referred to as AUC or AUROC, which is a scalar metric that may be used to compare the performance of two different classifieres. Note, however, that depending on the users requirement the classifier with the larger AUC may perform worse than the classifier with the smaller AUC. This can happen if the ROC curves of the two classifiers cross each other. E.g. one classifier may be best in most of the region and thus end up with the largest AUC, while still being outperformed in the a specific region such as very high positive rate.


Choosing a metric
All the above metrics are valid measures-of-goodness, but not all make sense in all cases. For a trivial example, consider precision. If this metric is used in the maintenance example from the utility section, the result would be very bad indeed. Since that metric prioritises a high purity among the instances classified as positive, but does not pay any regard to the instances classified as negative, a large false negative rate is likely. But this was exactly what needed to be avoided in this case, since a false negative would lead to a breakdown of the machinery and thus incur a large cost.
A slightly less obvious, but quite common and important, example of a bad choise of metric occurs when we have a large imbalance between the classes in the sample we want to classify. Say, positive class only constitute 1 permille of the total sample. If we use accuracy as our metric we would probably end up with a model that classifies all instances as negative, since this model would be 99.9% accurate. However, despite of the very high accuracy, the model is completely useless since none of the interesting instances are found.






NoteExercise



Your task is to make a machine learning algorithm that will classify a large set of chemical compounds as being either good candidates for becoming a new medicine (positive) or uninteresting for medical use (negative). The selected compounds will be taken into further testing to prove or disprove their applicability as a medicine. Find suitable metrics in the given scenarios:

Further testing is cheap, and the potential revenue of the new medicine is large.
Further testing is expensive, and the potiential revenue of the new medicine is modest.
Further testing is expensive, and the potenial revenue of the new medicine is large.

title: Evaluation metrics
Evaluation metrics
text:
Metrics for regression
Metrics for regression are typically an aggregate of the deviation between model prediction and correct value for all instances in the data set used for evaluation. Since both predicting a too high and a too low value is undesirable, one need to apply a function such that both cases contribute with a positive number in the aggregated value. In order to make the metric independent of number of instances used in the evaluation, one typically use the mean deviation.
Let \(\hat{y}_i\) be the predicted value corresponding to correct value \(y_i\).

Mean squared error (MSE) is a mean of the squared deviations from the correct value \[\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (\hat{y}_i-y_i)^2\]
Root mean squared error (RMSE) is the square root of MSE \[\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\text{MSE}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (\hat{y}_i-y_i)^2}\]
Mean absolute error (MAE) is the mean of the absolute values of the deviations from the correct value \[\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N |\hat{y}_i - y_i|\]


Choosing a metric
MSE and RMSE measure essentially the same thing, but there are nontheless important differences. MSE has the benefit that it is more easily differentiable, and is therefore a very good candidate for having the double use of both loss function and metric. RMSE, on the other hand, has - due to the square root after summing the squares - the same dimension as the input data. It is thus more easy to interpret what a particular value of RMSE means.

title: Uncertainty
text:
Whenever one wants to determine something about the world we live in, there is uncertainty involved. If you perform a measurement, there will only be a finite achievable precision. If you sample a population to evaluate something, no matter how well you design the study there is a possibility that your sample is not completely representative of the whole population (unless you can actually include the whole population in your sample). The uncertainty is not necessarily a problem, though. If you can control the uncertainty such that its magnitude is small enough to be irrelevant, all is well. And even if you can’t make the uncertainty as small as you would like, your results may be perfectly usable as long as you keep the uncertainty in mind. This is provided that you can actually quantify the uncertainty. There are well-established methods for quantifying, or at least estimating, the uncertainty of most physical measurements and also for combining the uncertainties of the input data when calculating a composite quantity. But when an ML model is involved, with its large number of internal parameters, it is less clear how to estimate the uncertainty of its output. There are (at least) two different problems we need to address concerning uncertainty relating to ML models. Firstly, there is propagation of uncertainty. Secondly, there is the challenge of evaluating extra uncertainty relating to the ML model itself.
Schematically what we want to achive can be illustrated like this:
Note that the output has a double set of error bars—one stemming from the uncertainty of the input data, and one from the inference process made by the ML model.
For at simple mathematical model combining a number of input parameters there is a well defined procedure to combine uncertainties, at least as long as they result from a known propability density function.1 If we have a quantity \(f\) which is determined from some measured quantities \(x_1, x_2, \ldots\), i.e. \[ f = f(x_1, x_2, \ldots) \] the uncertainty of \(f\), we’ll denote this as \(\sigma_f\), can be determined as \[ \sigma_f^2= \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}\right)^2\sigma_{x_1}^2 + \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}\right)^2\sigma_{x_2}^2 + \ldots + \text{correlation terms}\] where \(\sigma_{x_i}\) is the uncertainty of the measurment of \(x_i\). The correlation terms account for possible correlations between the different \(x_i\), and the exact form will depend on which distribution the \(x_i\)’s are taken from.
Since many popular ML models, including NN, produce a differentiable relation between the input and output the method above applies - at least in priciple. However, in problems where using an ML model is a sensible approach we typically have very many, and usually, correlated inputs. This makes the application of the above procedure cumbersome. Also, there are as we will discuss in the next section typically also sources of uncertainty which are not distributed following a simple probability density function, and then we clearly need another approach.
